title: Tsongkhapa
hook: the founder of the Gelug school: renunciation, bodhicitta, right view

segments.voice: Yesterday: Longchenpa and the mind's natural state, clear water once the stirring stops.

Out of everything you've ever been taught, if you could keep only three things, which would they be? Not three facts. Three things that hold the rest together. A Tibetan monk once answered that question for the whole Buddhist path. He wrote a long, careful book on the stages of the way to awakening. He also wrote a short poem that boils it down to three. Today, Tsongkhapa.
screen: `KEEP ONLY THREE THINGS.` → `A LONG BOOK ON THE PATH.` → `AND A SHORT POEM.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Tsongkhapa is remembered as the founder of the Gelug school. Tradition says he studied with teachers from several Tibetan lineages, prized monastic discipline and careful reasoning, and wrote the Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path. His short poem is called the Three Principal Aspects of the Path, and tradition says he wrote it as a letter to a student far away. Second, renunciation. Not throwing everything away, but a clear decision to be free: seeing that chasing one more comfort never ends the restlessness, and turning toward something steadier. Third, bodhicitta, the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings. Renunciation alone could become a private escape. Bodhicitta turns the journey outward, so the freedom sought is freedom for everyone, your neighbors included. Fourth, right view: understanding emptiness, that things arise in dependence on causes and do not stand on their own. Without it, the poem says, even renunciation and bodhicitta cannot cut the root of suffering. Put it in everyday terms. A traveler needs a reason to leave home, someone to make the trip for, and a true map. Leave out any one and the journey stalls. In the Gelug school, students learn this short text and come back to it, the long book folded into a pocket.
screen: `A LONG BOOK, AND A LETTER-POEM.` · `RENUNCIATION: DECIDING TO BE FREE.` · `BODHICITTA: FREEDOM FOR EVERYONE.` · `RIGHT VIEW: NOTHING STANDS ALONE.` · then, large: `A REASON, A PERSON, A MAP.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself three quiet questions, resting a few breaths with each: what do I want to be free of, who besides me would I want that freedom for, and what would I need to see clearly for any of it to work? Let the answers be short and honest, even unfinished, in your own words rather than Tsongkhapa's.
Tsongkhapa. The founder of the Gelug school, who folded the whole path into three principal aspects: renunciation, bodhicitta and right view. Today's word.
Your line: three principal things. A reason, a person, and a true map. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students in the Gelug school recite Tsongkhapa's Three Principal Aspects of the Path, hear it taught by their teachers, and study his Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path as a map of the whole way.

chat.says: What three things did Tsongkhapa say the whole path comes down to?
options: Renunciation, bodhicitta and right view: a reason, a person, a map.
Study, debate and discipline: master those and the path is complete.
Bodhicitta alone; with enough kindness, right view isn't needed.
chat.meaning: His poem names renunciation, bodhicitta and right view. Without right view, it says, even the other two cannot cut the root of suffering.

notes: Editor: removed the implied order (long book first, 'then' the poem) that the sources don't state; softened 'Gelug students memorize' to a non-sweeping line; changed the carry, which repeated day 968's 'write your three steps on paper'.

'Studied with teachers from several Tibetan lineages': general; confirm.
